turns.t: Good morning, Mr Whitcombe. The booking note says you've noticed black stools since starting ibuprofen. Is that right?
Good morning, doctor. Yes, that is right. I have been passing black stools, and it rather alarmed my wife.
I'm not surprised. Describe them for me. Is it like tar, or more a dark brown?
Quite like tar, I would say. Very dark, rather sticky, and unpleasant to flush away, if you will forgive me.
And when did you first notice it?
I'm afraid I cannot say with any confidence. Possibly last week, possibly the week before. I did not make a note.
That's fine, plenty of people don't. Now, tell me about the ibuprofen. Who started you on it?
My GP prescribed it for my knees. I take the 400 milligrams, I believe. The box is on the kitchen shelf, I'm afraid.
And how often are you meant to take them?
Three times a day, with food. I take them every day, though I must admit I often forget the lunchtime one.
Right. Think of ibuprofen as a bit of sandpaper on the lining of your stomach. Fine for a while, but it can wear that lining thin.
I see. I had rather assumed that taking it with food made it perfectly safe.
It helps a little, but it doesn't make it safe. Have you been sick at all?
No, not once. I have felt quite well in that respect.
Good. Any pain in the stomach, even a dull ache after meals?
No pain at all, which is partly why I put off coming.
Fair enough. What about dizziness, say when you stand up quickly?
No, I have been quite steady on my feet, thank you.
Is the ibuprofen your only regular medicine?
Yes, just that one. I try to avoid taking tablets where I can.
Any other health problems I should know about?
Osteoarthritis, which is the reason for the knees. And I have high cholesterol, but I manage that with diet.
Sensible. And how are the knees managing generally?
Stiff in the mornings, but they loosen up. Ibuprofen takes the edge off, I will say.
Understood. Any operations in the past?
One. I had a hernia repair, about twelve years ago. It went very smoothly.
You said you take it with food. Do you take it with a drink of any sort, milk or tea perhaps?
Just a cup of tea with my breakfast. Nothing more elaborate than that, I'm afraid.
Good. Let me check you over. I'll take your pulse and blood pressure first, then feel your tummy.
Of course. Shall I roll up my sleeve?
Yes please. Pulse is 92, blood pressure 118 over 74, oxygen level 98 percent, and your temperature is 36.8 degrees.
Are those numbers all right?
They're acceptable, nothing that worries me today. Now, lie back for me, and tell me if anything is sore.
Certainly. It's perfectly comfortable so far.
Your tummy feels soft all the way round, which is reassuring.
That is a relief. May I ask what happens now?
I'd rather not put a name on this just yet. But the first step is simple. Stop the ibuprofen from today.
Understood. Should I simply stop it altogether, or cut down?
Stop it altogether, and don't swap it for any similar painkiller from the chemist either. Those cause the same trouble.
I shall be careful about that. My knees may complain, I suppose.
They might, and we can talk about gentler options for them another time.
Thank you. Is there anything I should watch for in the meantime?
Yes. If the stools stay black, or you feel faint, or you bring up blood, go to A and E straight away.
I will, doctor. I'll let my wife know as well.
Good idea. She sounds sensible. Mind how you go, Mr Whitcombe.
Thank you very much. Good morning.

clinical_actions.description: Stop ibuprofen and avoid similar painkillers
Safety-net advice: attend A and E if stools stay black, faintness or vomiting blood

clinical_uncertainties.description: The patient cannot say when the black stools began.
The patient is not sure of the ibuprofen strength.
The patient says he takes it daily but often forgets the lunchtime dose.
